lifted.anchor: An operational definition can be perfectly precise and still be bad measurement.
**Reliability** is consistency.
**Validity** is accuracy.
One principle ties the two together
A pilot test is a trial run of the codebook before the real coding begins.
That word, independently, carries the whole logic.
The obvious way to turn the pilot into a number is to count how often the two coders matched.
It is also misleading, and seeing why is the key idea of the chapter.
Cohen's 1960 paper that introduced the standard fix made the point with a sharp example.
Raw agreement cannot tell that empty agreement apart from the real kind.
What you need is a measure that starts from the agreement actually observed
**Cohen's kappa** is the first, introduced in the 1960 paper just mentioned
When the coders do no better than chance, the numerator is zero
Either way the result is a number between roughly zero and one
To see what a failed check looks like, and why codebooks fail it
Imagine the codebook included a loosely worded variable.
The two coders agreed on 80 of the 100 messages
By the Landis and Koch labels, 0.015 is slight agreement
A kappa of 0.015 is not a result to report.
The fix begins with diagnosis.
Then the codebook, now revised, is piloted again.
This is why Chapter 9 finalized only the codebook's status
